### Issue description

I'm not actually sure if this is actually a bug, or just undocumented behavior, so there could be room for discussion.

At least through a quick search in the docs, I can't find any warning that `preload()` is unable to unload resources, and yet, [it is widely recommended as the default option in official docs pages](https://github.com/search?q=repo%3 …

This causes them to be pinned to memory for the entirety of the game's runtime, with no clear warning signs of how bad this can be.\n\nAs a consequence, if a game preloads heavy scenes, such as entire levels, a long session might cause the game to slow down or even crash, due to the continuous pile-up of resources that never get cleaned up by Godot.

That means using `preload()` is as dangerous as creating cyclic references between RefCounted objects, if not more because resources can contain large amounts of data.

Notes:
- This is not a memory leak, because the resources can still be loaded from the cache, so a specific resource won't be instantiated multiple times.
- This seems to be directly caused by #77513, since preloads are held by compiled scripts.
- Despite the similar name, the ResourcePreloader node is not affected by this.
Its resources are held by the scene resource, same as `@export` vars.

## Summary

This PoC adds support for discovering and using C# scripts defined in external assemblies referenced via `<ProjectReference>` or `<PackageReference>`.

Currently, Godot only scans the main project assembly for scripts, so `[Export]` properties, `[GlobalClass]`, and lifecycle methods (`_Ready`, `_Process`, etc.) do not work for types in referenced assemblies.\r\n\r\nMulti-project C# solutions are standard practice in .NET for code organization, shared libraries, and modular architecture.

This limitation has been reported across 25+ issues spanning 3 years since the .NET 6 migration.\r\n\r\n**Example project:** [GodotMultiAssemblyReference](https://github.com/matelq/GodotMultiAssemblyReference) — a complete working example with 3 assembly types (in-tree ProjectReference, in-tree Godot SDK ProjectReference, out-of-tree NuGet PackageReference).

Clone it and open with the patched engine to test.

### 2. `csharp://` path scheme for out-of-tree scripts

Scripts outside `res://` (NuGet packages, truly external projects) get a synthetic `csharp://AssemblyName/Namespace.ClassName.cs` path. `ResourceFormatLoaderCSharpScript::load()` handles these by skipping source file loading and registering directly with `ScriptServer`.

**Open question:** Is introducing a new URI scheme the right approach?
Alternatives considered: `res://.godot/external/` stub files (rejected — creates physical files on disk), extending `res://` to support `../` paths (rejected — security implications).\r\n\r\n### 3.

Recommended project layout

The PoC works best when `project.godot` is placed at the solution root:

```
MyGame/ <- project.godot here (res:// root)
 project.godot <- dotnet/project/project_directory = "MainProject"
 MainProject/
 MyGame.csproj
 Player.cs <- res://MainProject/Player.cs
 Modules/
 Combat/
 Combat.csproj
 HealthComponent.cs <- res://Modules/Combat/HealthComponent.cs
 MyGame.slnx
```

This keeps all module source files under `res://` with full editor integration.

A new `dotnet/project/project_directory` setting supports `.csproj` in a subdirectory.

**Open question:** Is this layout acceptable as the recommended pattern, or should the engine be more flexible about project structures?

### 4.

Other changes

- `_register_csharp_global_class()` helper consolidates 3 duplicated registration blocks in `csharp_script.cpp`
- `property_utils.cpp` stores/retrieves `csharp://` paths as `_custom_type_script` meta (no UID)
- `ResourceFormatSaverCSharpScript::recognize()` rejects `csharp://` scripts
- MSBuild `Sdk.targets` propagates `GodotProjectDir` to `ProjectReference` items
- `InspectorPlugin` and `GodotSharpEditor` handle `csharp://` gracefully
- Generic type virtual paths (`csharp://path:GenericType`) disambiguated with `FileAccess::exists()` fallback

The `csharp://` path scheme is minimal — it enables `[GlobalClass]` and `[Export]` without changes to Godot's core resource system.

The infrastructure (assembly scanning, `csharp://` loader) could be extended to support PCK-based modding in the future.\r\n\r\nI understand that a GDExtension migration ([godot-proposals#7895](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7895)) may ultimately provide a more integrated solution.

This PoC aims to solve the immediate need that users have had for 3+ years, in a way that's backward compatible and could coexist with or be replaced by a GDExtension approach.

The internal orientation value updates, but the device screen stays in whatever orientation it was at launch.

This is an iOS-only regression introduced by the SwiftUI lifecycle migration in Godot 4.6.

---

#### What happens

1.

Call `DisplayServer.screen_set_orientation(SCREEN_LANDSCAPE)` at runtime
2. `screen_orientation` is stored correctly ✅
3. `setNeedsUpdateOfSupportedInterfaceOrientations` is called ✅
4. **iOS does not rotate the screen** ❌

On Android, the exact same code works — the screen physically rotates.

---

#### Root cause

**PR #109974** (Godot 4.6) migrated iOS to the SwiftUI lifecycle.

Since the `UIHostingController` (root) doesn't override this method, it returns the default mask and iOS ignores the orientation change.\n\nBefore the SwiftUI migration, `AppDelegate.viewController` was the root VC directly, so PR #78132's fix worked.

After #109974, the same call targets the wrong VC.

**Secondary issue:** On iOS 16+, calling `setNeedsUpdateOfSupportedInterfaceOrientations` alone does not force rotation when the device is held still. `UIWindowScene.requestGeometryUpdateWithPreferences:` must also be called to trigger the physical rotation.

---

#### Timeline of related changes

| PR | What it did | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **#78132** (2023) | Added `setNeedsUpdateOfSupportedInterfaceOrientations` call to `screen_set_orientation()`.

Worked because `AppDelegate.viewController` was the root VC. | ✅ Fixed at the time |\n| **#109974** (2025) | Migrated iOS to SwiftUI lifecycle. `GDTViewController` became a child of `UIHostingController`. | ⚠️ Broke orientation |\n| **#109478** (2025) | Restored accidentally deleted `screen_orientation = p_orientation;` line.
Set `display/window/handheld/orientation = 6` (Sensor) in Project Settings\n2.

Add a Button with script:
 ```gdscript
 func _on_pressed():
 DisplayServer.screen_set_orientation(DisplayServer.SCREEN_LANDSCAPE)
 ```
3.
Export to an iOS device (iPhone or iPad)\n4.
Launch the app holding the device in portrait\n5.

Tap the button

**Expected:** Screen physically rotates to landscape (as it does on Android)
**Actual:** `screen_orientation` updates internally but the device screen stays in portrait

### Minimal reproduction project (MRP)

Reproducible with any project that calls `screen_set_orientation()` on iOS with Godot 4.6.x.

The detection can only be prevented by setting Area2D.monitoring = false (Note: it's not .monitable property.).

The behavior is different in Godot 4, that when Area2D sets a collision bit and CharacterBody2D sets a corresponding mask, the detection does not happen anymore.


### Note before continuing

This issue can have two interpretations, that a) it's a designd change that Godot 4 intentionally prevent CharacterBody2D detecting Area2D, just didn't explain in documentation, or b) it can be a Godot 3 quirk because .monitoring property does not seems to affect this behavior.

Given there's a clear workaround (described below), it should be a low priority issue, but a confirmation of expected behavior is needed.


### Use case scenario

I've devel …
The enemy supports two behaviors:\r\n- An Enemy can be defeated by player.
Once defeated, enemy is still placed on map.

Player can't collide with it.
- A defeated enemy can be reactivated by an effect released by other enemies, say, flame.

In Godot 3, this feature is implemented by settings collision bits.
A brief setup looks like below:\r\n\r\n- Enemy is an KinematicBody2D node with GDScript.
In normal state, it calls set_collision_layer_bit(ENEMY, true).

When it's defeated, it calls set_collision_layer_bit(ENEMY, false) and set_collision_mask_bit(FLAME, true).
- Flame is an Area2D node, with $Area2D.set_collision_layer_bit(FLAME, true).

With setup above, player does not collide with a defeated enemy (it has no collision layer bit).
The defeated enemy responds to flame (KinematicBody2D sets mask bit while Area2D sets layer bit).
Requirements are met.\r\n\r\nHowever, when migrating my game to Godot 4 with same setup, the defeated enemy does not respond to flame.
When I calls $CharacterBody2D.set_collision_layer_value(ENEMY, true) and $Area2D.set_collision_mask_value(ENEMY, true), the defeated enemy responds to both flame and player.

Neither is expected.

### Workaround in Godot 4

A workaround is to add a new collision layer, DEFEATED_ENEMY. 
- When enemy is defeated, it sets collision layer to DEFEATED_ENEMY while in normal case it sets collision layer to ENEMY.
- Flame sets collision mask DEFEATED_ENEMY.
- Player sets collision mask to ENEMY.

When an enemy is defeated, player does not collide with enemy (because player collides with ENEMY but not DEFEATED_ENEMY), while flame can reactivate enemy (because it detects DEFEATED_ENEMY).

Side effect of the workaround: The layer/mask bits are limited to 32 slots.
It needs to be shared between terrain, characters and players.

Adding more complicated interactions for enemies with different skills can exhaust the slots.

This happens with both classes (nullable) and with primitives/value types (not nullable).\r\n\r\nHere's an example of an affected function.
The line `var point := intersection as Vector3` now produces the error `Casting \"Variant\" to \"Vector3\" is unsafe.

This means that result of `type_convert` (e.g. `type_convert(intersection, TYPE_VECTOR3)` per the above example) also cannot be used type-safely except via, again, an implicit cast.\r\n\r\nI think there really needs to be a way to explicitly convert a Variant to another typed value that does not produce a type safety error.

And at some point there should probably be an UNSAFE_IMPLICIT_CAST error so that these implicit casts can also be configured to generate errors.\r\n\r\nIdeally I would like very much to see nullable types merged for 4.3 and for casts from Variant to any nullable type to be considered safe (producing null if the Variant did not contain a value of the type being explicitly cast to), e.g. `variant_value as Vector3?` and casting to non-nullable value types to be unsafe.

But until nullable types are a thing, I would rather still be able to write `variant_value as [Type]` to explicitly mark intentional casts, rather than be required to use implicit casts to work around the error, or have to turn the UNSAFE_CAST error/warning off entirely and lose its benefits in other situations. https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/76843

In my opinion, adding built-in functions such as `int_convert`, `float_convert`, `vector3_convert`, etc. for each possible type to use instead of casting with `as` would also be an acceptable resolution, albeit not an ideal one, with these functions returning the corresponding types directly rather than returning a Variant as with `type_convert`.

Rather than enforcing a specific way to save games, it provides the robust infrastructure (singleton, threading, encryption, integrity) that developers currently have to build from scratch.\r\n\r\nThis system evolves Godot's persistence into a **\"Git for Gameplay\"** model, where instead of full memory dumps, we store **State Increments**.

This allows for massive performance gains, atomic updates, and global node identification that survives hierarchy changes.

## The Problem

Saving game state in Godot right now is... tedious.
Even for something simple like player health and position, you end up writing a lot of boilerplate.

You manually build dictionaries, serialize to JSON or binary, handle file I/O, and if you want to avoid frame drops during autosave, you need to implement your own threading. Want encryption? Checksums?
Backup files in case of corruption?
That's all on you.\r\n\r\nI've seen this pattern repeated in almost every Godot project I've worked on or reviewed.
Everyone writes their own `SaveManager` class with `save_game()` and `load_game()` methods.
It works, but it's repetitive and error-prone.

New developers especially struggle with this - it's one of those \"figure it out yourself\" areas where the engine doesn't provide much guidance.\r\n\r\nUsing `ResourceSaver` to save entire scenes is overkill for most cases - you don't want to save the entire scene structure, just the dynamic state.

But manually tracking which properties need saving is annoying and easy to forget when you add new features.

## Proposal

The core idea is simple: let developers mark properties as persistent, and the engine handles the rest.

### 1.
The `@persistent` Annotation System\r\n\r\nThe core idea is simple: mark properties for automatic saving.

The system is flexible, supporting tags, groups, and native integration with `@export` on any `Object` (Nodes or Resources).

```gdscript
extends CharacterBody3D

# --- Basic ---
# Automatically saved to the snapshot
@persistent var player_name: String = "Hero"

# --- Editor Integration (@export) ---
# Designers set initial value in editor.

Allows saving ONLY this later:
# SaveServer.save_snapshot(root, "slot_1", true, ["inventory"])
# This creates a satellite file 'slot_1_inventory.tres' linked to the main manifest.
@persistent("inventory") var items: Array = []

# --- Groups (Syntactic Sugar) ---
# Clean way to apply "progression" tag to multiple variables
@persistent_group("progression")
@persistent var level: int = 1
@persistent var experience: int = 0
```

This completely eliminates the need for manual dictionaries or custom `ResourceSaver` logic.

**Advanced Use Cases:**
Since it works at the object level, you can preserve volatile state that is usually lost, like audio playback:

The Snapshot Resource\r\n\r\nThe `Snapshot` class is a new `Resource` type that encapsulates saved game state.

It serves as the container format for all save files, whether text or binary.

**Properties:**

- **`snapshot`** (Dictionary): The actual game state data collected from persistent properties and `_save_persistence()` calls
- **`tag_slots`** (Dictionary): Maps tags to additional slot files (Satellite support).
- **`version`** (String): The game version when this save was created (from `application/config/version`)
- **`metadata`** (Dictionary): Lightweight data for UI display (playtime, level name, character name, etc.)
- **`thumbnail`** (Texture2D): Optional screenshot taken at save time
- **`checksum`** (String): SHA-256 hash of the snapshot data for integrity validation

The separation of `metadata` from `snapshot` is crucial for performance.

When displaying a save file list in the UI, you can load just the metadata and thumbnail without deserializing the entire game state:

```gdscript
# Load menu can show save info without loading full state
var save_info = SaveServer.get_save_metadata("slot_1")
$Label.text = "%s - Level %d - %s" % [
 save_info["character_name"],
 save_info["level"],
 save_info["playtime"]
]
$TextureRect.texture = save_info["thumbnail"]
```

This design mirrors how modern games display save file information instantly, without the loading delays that would come from deserializing gigabytes of game state just to show a preview.

### 4.
The `SaveServer` Singleton\r\n\r\nA new core singleton responsible for orchestrating the save process.

It acts similarly to `AudioServer` or `PhysicsServer`, delegating the heavy work to a dedicated system.

Basic usage would look like this:

```gdscript
# Save the entire game state starting from the root node
await SaveServer.save_snapshot(get_tree().root, "save_slot_1")

# Load it back
SaveServer.load_snapshot(get_tree().root, "save_slot_1")
```

## Why This Matters

I think this would be a huge quality-of-life improvement for Godot.
Save systems are one of those things that every non-trivial game needs, but the engine doesn't really help with.

You either spend time building your own infrastructure or you ship with a fragile JSON-based system and hope for the best.\r\n\r\nHaving this built-in would put Godot ahead of Unity (which has nothing like this) and on par with Unreal's save game system, but simpler to use.

More importantly, it would let developers - especially newer ones - focus on making their game instead of debugging why their save file got corrupted.\r\n\r\nThe Object-level implementation makes it flexible enough for any use case, from simple platformers to complex RPGs with thousands of persistent entities.
